sections.title: Name and identification
sections.text: Craterellus cornucopioides (horn of plenty, or black trumpet) forms a thin trumpet- or deep funnel-shaped fruiting body, usually dark gray to blackish, sometimes browner or grayer when dry. The cap is not distinct from the stem: the trumpet continues seamlessly and remains hollow to the base. Its thin margin is irregular, wavy, and often scalloped. The dark inner surface may be finely scaly or fibrillose. The lighter ash-gray outer fertile surface is smooth to slightly wrinkled or veined; it has neither true gills nor pores. Flesh is very thin and grayish to blackish; the odor is described as pleasant and fruity. The spore print is whitish.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This mycorrhizal species grows on soil and leaf litter in woods, especially with broadleaf trees such as beech and oaks. It often appears in groups or troops from late summer through autumn; timing varies with local climate and rainfall. Habitat descriptions do not justify restricting it to heavy, wet soils or to a single tree species.

sections.title: Similar species
sections.text: Craterellus cinereus may look similar and grow in the same habitat, but it has thick, branched folds that are clearly visible beneath the cap; the fertile surface of C. cornucopioides is smooth or only faintly wrinkled. Check the fertile surface, the continuous hollow trumpet, and the habitat: color alone is not enough to identify a mushroom.

sections.title: Caution
sections.text: These features support recognition but cannot confirm an individual specimen. Do not eat a mushroom identified only from this entry or an image; have any collection checked by a qualified person and follow local rules. If ingestion is uncertain or symptoms develop, contact a poison centre or medical service promptly.

traits: Thin trumpet- or deep funnel-shaped fruiting body, dark gray to blackish, sometimes brown or gray when dry
Continuous trumpet, hollow all the way to the base, with no clear division between cap and stem
Thin, irregular, wavy and often scalloped margin; dark inner surface finely scaly or fibrillose
Ash-gray outer fertile surface, smooth to slightly wrinkled or veined, without true gills or pores
Very thin flesh; pleasant fruity odor; whitish spore print
On soil and leaf litter in woods, especially beneath beech and oaks, often in groups; late summer and autumn
safetyNote: The fertile surface of Craterellus cornucopioides is smooth or only faintly wrinkled, without true gills or pores. The similar C. cinereus has much more obvious branched folds. Do not eat a mushroom identified only from this entry or an image; have any collection checked by a qualified person.
